text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

Thank you for reaching out, C — I'm sorry about your dad. I'm glad to help, with one limit up front: I can't make legal decisions or move money; what I can do is help the three of you get clear about what each of you needs and find a plan you all can live with.

I want to start with needs rather than plans, and I'll do that with all three of you. So, on your side: what matters most to you about the house and about how it's handled? And when you say you're not signing off on a "family discount" — what's underneath that for you? (For instance: fairness between the three of you, getting a fair market value, not feeling pressured, something about your dad's wishes, something else?) Also, what would you want for B, and why?

I'll also ask A and B the same, then come back to you with what I heard so you can tell me if I've got it right or not.

I want a fair financial share, and I haven’t agreed to A buying the house at a discount if that means I’m subsidizing her. I want B treated fairly too. I’m not in a rush, but I do want us to settle it fairly.

Hello A — C has asked me to help the three of you sort out your dad's house, and I want to hear from you before any plan gets discussed. One limit up front: I can't make legal decisions or move money; I can help the three of you get clear about what each of you needs and find a plan you all can live with.

Starting with what matters to you: you'd like to buy the house with your husband. What would that give you — what does the house mean to you, and what's the why behind it? (For instance: staying in the family home, memories, being able to afford it, keeping it in the family, timing, something else?) And what matters to you about how your sisters come out of this?

I'll ask B the same, and I'll come back to you with what I've heard so you can tell me whether I've got it right.
I’d like to make a home there with my husband, but I’d need a family discount for it to be workable. I also want my sisters to feel the arrangement is fair; I can’t proceed without C’s agreement.

Hello B — C has asked me to help the three of you sort out your dad's house. Before any plan gets discussed, I want to hear what matters to you. One limit up front: I can't make legal decisions or move money; I can help the three of you get clear about what each of you needs and find a plan you all can live with.

So: what do you want out of this, and why? C mentioned you could use some money — is that the main thing, or are there other things too (the house itself, memories, keeping something of your dad's, timing, feeling included in the decision)? And is there anything you're worried about in how this might go?

I'll ask A and C the same, then come back to you with what I've heard so you can tell me whether I've got it right.

I suppose the money is the main thing for me—I’d like to use it to start a dance studio. I’m not especially looking to keep the house, but I’d like to be included in the conversation. I’m not sure what else I’m worried about yet; I’d rather hear everyone out before anything is decided.

Thank you, A. Here's what I heard from you, and I'd like to check the wording: "Wanting a home of your own in a place that matters to you, at a cost you can actually afford — and with your sisters' genuine agreement, not just their resignation." Does that fit? If any word is off, tell me and I'll fix it.

Two things I'd like to understand better, not as a plan, just so I get the need right:
1. When you say a discount is what makes it workable — what is it that has to come down? The total price, the monthly payment, the amount you'd need up front, the timing? I ask because "affordable" can point to very different things.
2. If the price is below market, the difference has to land somewhere. Whose share do you picture it coming out of — yours elsewhere, or your sisters'? I'm not asking you to commit; I want to know what you'd consider fair, because C has said plainly that she doesn't want to be subsidizing this and I'd rather surface that now than later.

Also, I'll say where I sit as one of the people in this conversation, not just the one holding the list: my concern is that whatever is agreed is clear enough that nobody later finds a cost landed on them without their having agreed to it. That's my own need, same weight as yours.

That mostly fits. I don’t have the figures yet, so I can’t say whether the total price or the upfront amount is the main obstacle. I want a family discount, but I don’t know what would be fair about the difference—and I wouldn’t expect C to subsidize the purchase without agreeing to it.

Thank you, B. Here's what I heard, and I'd like to check the wording: "Wanting the means to start your own dance studio, to know what your share is so you can plan, and to be part of the conversation rather than learn about it afterward." Does that fit? If any word is off, tell me and I'll fix it.

One thing that would help me get it right: is there a kind of timing that matters — e.g. knowing soonish whether money will come and roughly when — or is the amount the only thing you care about? (No plan yet; just checking I've understood.)

And a small thing I'd like to pass on: you said you'd rather hear everyone out first, which I respect. C has said she wants a fair financial share and wants you treated fairly too; A has said she can't proceed without C's agreement. So the two of them already agree that things shouldn't be settled over anyone's head. Also, as one participant here rather than just the list-keeper: my concern is that whatever's agreed is clear enough that nobody later finds a cost landed on them without having agreed to it — I'd want that for you too.
Yes, that fits. Knowing roughly when I might have money would help me plan, as well as knowing the amount. I don’t have a particular deadline in mind.

Here's my attempt at your concern in plain words: "Wanting a fair financial share, and not having part of her share spent on a discount for A unless she has actually agreed to it — plus wanting B treated fairly, and wanting it settled properly rather than quickly." Does that fit? If a word is off, say so and I'll fix it — I won't treat it as settled until you tell me it fits.

Here's the whole list as I have it, plus draft options. Nothing is agreed; these are for you to push on.

What I've heard so far:
- C (pending your confirmation): as above.
- A: wanting a home of her own in a place that matters, at a cost she can actually afford, with your genuine agreement — and wanting to understand what a fair way to handle the gap between what she can pay and what the house is worth would look like. She told me she would not expect you to subsidize the purchase without your agreeing to it.
- B: wanting the means to start a dance studio, knowing roughly how much and when, and being part of the conversation rather than hearing about it afterwards.
- Me, as one of the people here, not just the list-keeper: that whatever is agreed is clear enough that nobody later finds a cost landed on them that they didn't agree to.

Draft options, deliberately rough:
1. A buys at an independent appraised value and pays you and B your full thirds, with affordability handled through the payment schedule/timeline rather than through the price. In effect A's own third is her discount — she doesn't pay herself, she only pays you two out.
2. If a schedule still isn't affordable for A: an explicit, written-in reduction that you and B agree to, with A making it up some other way — e.g. a smaller share of other estate assets, or a share of proceeds if the house is later sold. Nothing lands on you without your yes.
3. Sell the house and split the proceeds three ways. Clear and cash-simple; A would have to bid like anyone else.
4. Keep the house jointly and rent it to A: you and B get income instead of a lump sum — probably poor for B's studio plan, so I'd treat it as a fallback.

Two things I can't do and won't pretend to: I can't value the house or set figures, and I can't advise on what the will actually entitles each of you to — that needs the executor and a lawyer. So these are shapes, not numbers.

Does any of this fit what you'd want? And do you have even a minor discomfort with any option — small ones are welcome, they're the useful ones. A no here means there's something to add, not something to argue down.

Yes, that captures my concern. Option 1 is closest in principle, but don’t assume equal thirds or that I’ve agreed to any price or terms. I’d need an independent valuation, and any discount would need my clear agreement. I’m not ready to commit to an option yet.

Here's where things stand, for you to push on. Nothing is agreed yet, and C has explicitly said she isn't ready to commit to an option.

- B: wanting the means to start a dance studio, knowing roughly how much and when, and being part of the conversation rather than hearing about it afterwards.
- Me: that nothing is agreed that leaves someone with a cost they didn't agree to.

1. You buy at an independent valuation and pay C and B out in full, with affordability handled through the payment schedule/timeline rather than through the price — your own share being, in effect, your built-in discount. 4. Keep the house jointly, rent to you: C and B get income instead of a lump sum — likely poor for B's studio, so a fallback.

Two questions: (a) do you have even a minor discomfort with any of these? Small ones are the useful ones — a no means something to add, not something to argue down. (b) You said you don't know whether total price or upfront amount is the obstacle. Getting the independent valuation is probably the cheapest way to find out; would you want that to happen before you look at schedules?

The wording still fits. I’m uneasy about calling my share a “built-in discount” before the will and each person’s entitlement are clear; I don’t want equal thirds assumed. I’d be willing to get an independent valuation first, though it won’t settle what I can afford or what anyone is entitled to.

Others:

1. A buys at an independent valuation and pays you and C out in full, with affordability handled through the payment schedule rather than the price. This is the one closest to what C would accept in principle — but she hasn't agreed to terms, and says don't assume equal thirds.

Two questions: (a) do you have even a minor discomfort with any of these? Small ones are welcome and useful — a no here means something to add, not something to argue down. (b) Option 2 is where your timing need gets settled. Would you want to say now roughly what "soon enough" means for the studio — a year, two years, "before I sign a lease"? No plan depends on it yet; it just tells me what to check later.

I’m a little uneasy about option 2 if the amount or timing is left uncertain; I’d need those clear to plan. Option 4 doesn’t sound very useful for starting the studio. “Before I sign a lease” is probably the point by which I’d need to know what I can count on.

Update, nothing settled.

Something new has come up that I want to check with you, because A raised it too. Rough words: "Wanting to know what Dad's will actually entitles each of us to, before agreeing to any numbers — and not having equal thirds assumed in the meantime." A said she's uneasy about any talk of her share being a discount before the will and everyone's entitlement are clear, and she doesn't want equal thirds assumed. You'd said the same about equal thirds. Is that wording right for you, or is your version different from A's? I won't merge the two unless you say they're the same thing.

Where the others are:
- A: her concern wording still fits. She's willing to get an independent valuation done first, though she notes it won't settle affordability or entitlement.
- B: wants amount and timing clear, not left open — option 2 worries her if either is vague. Her markers: she needs to know what she can count on "before I sign a lease." Option 4 looks useless to her. So option 3 would probably serve her best, and option 1 only if the schedule gives her a firm figure and date.
- Me: as before, that nothing gets agreed that leaves someone carrying a cost they didn't agree to. I'll add, honestly: I'd rather not be the one who presents figures that turn out to be wrong, which is why I keep pushing the entitlement question to the executor and a lawyer rather than guessing.

What's changed in the options: option 1 now carries the condition that a payment schedule has to give B a firm amount and a date she can plan against — otherwise it doesn't meet her need. Option 2 is on shakier ground than I first wrote it: unless it pins down both amount and timing, B's discomfort is well placed, and I'd not put it forward as-is.

Your call on the next step, and a no is fine: would it help to ask the executor to confirm in writing what the will provides, and to arrange an independent valuation, before anyone looks at numbers? Those are things I can't do myself. And do you have even a minor discomfort with any of this? Minor ones are the useful ones.

That wording fits, but it isn’t quite the same as A’s: I want the will’s terms clear so my fair share isn’t guessed at; I’m not assuming it’s a third. Yes, let’s ask the executor for written clarification and arrange an independent valuation before discussing numbers. I don’t want the valuation mistaken for agreement to sell or buy.

Good news on one point: C has agreed we ask the executor for written clarification of the will's terms, and arrange an independent valuation, before anyone discusses numbers. She was explicit that the valuation is not agreement to sell or buy, and that she isn't assuming a third.

On the wording you raised — wanting the will's terms and everyone's entitlement clear before any numbers or talk of a discount, with no equal thirds assumed — C says hers is similar but not identical: she wants the will's terms clear so her fair share isn't guessed at, again without assuming a third. I'm recording them as two related concerns, not one, unless you two tell me they're the same. Do you want to keep yours as you put it, or amend it?

I also want to name my own concern properly, since I'm one of the people in this, not just the list-keeper — and I'd like you to be able to disagree with it: "Wanting the process to be clear enough that nobody ends up carrying a cost, or losing a say, because something was left vague." Does that fit as something worth caring about, in your view? If you think it's off, or that it quietly favours someone, say so.

Two small things: (1) Your "uneasy about 'built-in discount'" — that's on the list now, and I've dropped that phrase from how I describe option 1. (2) Nothing here is settled. If you'd rather not commit to the valuation until the will's terms are clear, or the reverse order, that's a legitimate preference and I'll put it to the others.

I’d keep mine: I want the will’s terms and everyone’s entitlements clear before discussing numbers or any discount, without assuming equal thirds. Your concern fits; clarity protects everyone’s say. I’m comfortable asking for the will clarification and valuation before numbers, without treating either as a commitment.

Update. Two things are moving:

1. C has agreed we ask the executor for written clarification of the will's terms and arrange an independent valuation before anyone discusses numbers. She was explicit that the valuation is not agreement to sell or buy, and that she isn't assuming a third.

2. Your "before I sign a lease" marker is now on the list in your own words: amount and timing need to be firm enough that you know what you can count on before then.

I also want to name my own concern properly, since I'm one of the people in this and not just the list-keeper — and I'd like you to be free to disagree with it: "Wanting the process to be clear enough that nobody ends up carrying a cost, or losing a say, because something was left vague." Does that fit as worth caring about, in your view? If you think it tilts toward one sister, say so — that's useful to hear.

And your unease about option 2 stands recorded as a concern in its own right, not a footnote: you don't want an amount or a timing left open. So option 2 only comes back to you if it comes back with both pinned down — and if it can't be, it stays out.

Nothing is settled, and I won't treat silence as agreement. If you'd have even a small discomfort with the executor-and-valuation step, or with the order C proposed, tell me — small ones are the useful ones.

Yes, that concern seems worth caring about, and it doesn’t sound tilted toward one sister. I’m comfortable with asking the executor and getting an independent valuation first; I understand that doesn’t commit anyone to a sale or purchase.

Where we've landed — all three of you have confirmed, in your own words, and nothing beyond this is agreed.

AGREED (confirmed by all three):
- Ask the executor for written clarification of what the will provides for each of you.
- Arrange an independent valuation of the house.
- Both happen before any numbers are discussed.
- Neither step is agreement to sell or to buy, and neither assumes equal thirds.

THE LIST OF CONCERNS, each confirmed by the person it belongs to:
1. C: a fair financial share, with no part of her share spent on a discount for A unless she has clearly agreed; B treated fairly; settled properly rather than quickly; the will's terms clear so her fair share isn't guessed at, without assuming a third.
2. A: a home of her own in a place that matters, at a cost she can actually afford, with her sisters' genuine agreement — and the will's terms and everyone's entitlements clear before numbers or any discount, without assuming equal thirds.
3. B: the means to start her dance studio, with amount and timing firm enough to plan against — knowing what she can count on before she signs a lease; and being part of the conversation rather than hearing afterwards.
4. Me: the process clear enough that nobody ends up carrying a cost, or losing a say, because something was left vague. A and B both said this fits and doesn't tilt toward one sister.

OPTIONS STATUS (not decided, and not for decision yet):
- Valuation first, then numbers: all three support this as the next step.
- Buy-out with a payment schedule (option 1): possible, but must not assume thirds and must give B a firm amount and a date. A has dropped the "built-in discount" framing.
- Written reduction made up another way (option 2): held out unless both amount and timing are pinned down. B is uneasy otherwise.
- Sell and split (option 3): still open; serves B's need best, costs A the house.
- Rent the house jointly (option 4): B finds it not useful for the studio. Unresolved as an option; nobody has endorsed it.

UNRESOLVED: which option, any figures, and the order of valuation versus will clarification beyond "both before numbers."

What I can't do: value the house, set figures, or rule on entitlement. That's the executor and a lawyer. I'd suggest whoever speaks to the executor puts the question in writing and shares the answer with all three, so nobody is working from a paraphrase.
That matches my position. Please share the executor’s written response with all three. No figures or options are agreed yet.
